sections.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions (ITF) Domains & Ranges
sections.content: ITFs are only valid within restricted domains (Principal Value Branches) to ensure they are one-to-one. y = sin⁻¹(x) has domain [-1, 1] and range [-π/2, π/2]. y = cos⁻¹(x) has domain [-1, 1] and range [0, π].

sections.title: ITF Properties with Negative Arguments
sections.content: sin⁻¹(-x) = -sin⁻¹(x), tan⁻¹(-x) = -tan⁻¹(x), csc⁻¹(-x) = -csc⁻¹(x). However, cos⁻¹(-x) = π - cos⁻¹(x), sec⁻¹(-x) = π - sec⁻¹(x), and cot⁻¹(-x) = π - cot⁻¹(x).

sections.title: Composition of Trig and Inverse Trig
sections.content: sin(sin⁻¹x) = x for x ∈ [-1, 1]. BUT sin⁻¹(sin x) = x ONLY if x ∈ [-π/2, π/2]. If x is outside this branch, use allied angle properties to bring it back into the principal range before evaluating.

sections.title: ITF Addition Formulas
sections.content: tan⁻¹(x) + tan⁻¹(y) = tan⁻¹[(x+y)/(1-xy)] if xy < 1. If x>0, y>0, and xy > 1, the formula becomes π + tan⁻¹[(x+y)/(1-xy)].

sections.title: Properties of Triangles (Sine and Cosine Rules)
sections.content: Sine Rule: a/sinA = b/sinB = c/sinC = 2R (where R is circumradius). Cosine Rule: a² = b² + c² - 2bc*cosA, which is used to find angles when all three sides are known.

sections.title: Area, Inradius, and Exradii
sections.content: Area Δ = (1/2)ab*sinC = √(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)) (Heron's). Inradius r = Δ/s. Circumradius R = abc/4Δ. Exradius r1 = Δ/(s-a).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
1) Writing sin⁻¹(sin(2π/3)) = 2π/3. (Wrong, because 2π/3 is out of [-π/2, π/2]. Correct is π/3).
2) Using tan⁻¹(x) + tan⁻¹(y) formula without checking if xy > 1.
3) Confusing Inradius (r) formulas with Circumradius (R) formulas.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 3 delves into Inverse Trigonometry (strict domain/range rules, conversions) and Solutions of Triangles (linking trig to geometry via Sine/Cosine rules, incircles, and circumcircles).

tricks.title: Right Triangle Trick for ITF Conversion
tricks.explanation: To convert sin⁻¹ to cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹, draw a right triangle, assign perpendicular and hypotenuse, calculate base, and write the new ITF directly.
tricks.example: Convert sin⁻¹(3/5). Triangle: P=3, H=5 → Base=4. So, it equals tan⁻¹(3/4) and cos⁻¹(4/5).

tricks.title: The 'π' Adjustment for ITF Addition
tricks.explanation: Always multiply x and y before applying the tan⁻¹ addition formula. If the product is > 1 (and both are positive), instantly add π.

tricks.title: Telescoping Series in ITF
tricks.explanation: For series like Σ tan⁻¹(something), rewrite the argument to look like (x-y)/(1+xy). This transforms it into tan⁻¹(x) - tan⁻¹(y), allowing massive cancellation.

tricks.title: Half-Angle Tangent Substitution
tricks.explanation: Expressions with √(1-x²), √(1+x²), etc., inside an ITF are best solved by substituting x = sinθ, cosθ, or tanθ.

tricks.title: Sine Rule Proportionality
tricks.explanation: Because a = 2R*sinA, you can often treat sides a, b, c as directly proportional to sinA, sinB, sinC in ratio problems to simplify algebra.
tricks.example: If asked to find ratio of sides a:b:c for angles 30:60:90, it's just sin30:sin60:sin90 = 1 : √3 : 2.

tricks.title: m-n Theorem (Properties of Triangles)
tricks.explanation: If a point D divides side BC of ΔABC in ratio m:n, and angle ADC = θ, then: (m+n)cotθ = m cotα - n cotβ (where α, β are split angles at A) = n cotB - m cotC.
tricks.example: Instantly solves median/altitude angle problems where standard Sine/Cosine rules become too messy.
